strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: the lack of an objective, interpretable metric for evaluating and rewarding stylistic consistency in role-play TTS, as opposed to coarse emotion-classification rewards used in prior work.
The proposed MCLP metric is conceptually simple and practically implementable using a pretrained LALM's own ICL/continuation capability, without requiring additional labeled style categories.

The composite reward with CER gating is empirically well-motivated; the reward-hacking ablation (style-only vs. content-only optimization) convincingly demonstrates the necessity of the hybrid design and gating mechanism.

A new, reasonably large (1,435h, ~311k scenes) real-world multi-turn RP-TTS dataset with scene and character annotations is constructed via a non-trivial pipeline (diarization, scene segmentation, VLM/LLM annotation), which could be a useful community resource if released.

Evaluation combines objective metrics (CER, Pinyin WER, MCLP) with a subjective MOS study and an explicit human-correlation analysis (win-rate vs. ΔMCLP) that provides some validation that MCLP tracks human perception of style.
Consistent and large improvements over multiple strong baselines (GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio, Step-Audio-2-mini) in both content fidelity and stylistic MOS.
weaknesses: The information-theoretic justification (Eqs. 2-3) is largely decorative rather than rigorous: the step from mutual information to 'E[MCLP] ∝ ... ≈ -H(Z^gt|Z^eval) + KL(P_data||P_theta)' conflates proportionality and approximation without formal derivation, and the crucial assumption that the pretrained LALM is a 'strong density estimator' with small KL divergence is asserted, not empirically verified.

MCLP is fundamentally a reference-based (ground-truth-conditioned) metric, which conflates 'style fidelity to a single realization' with genuine stylistic quality; since expressive speech style is inherently one-to-many, this could penalize valid but different stylistic renditions and may partly explain the metric's behavior as a similarity/overfitting signal rather than an independent style-quality estimator. This limitation is not discussed.

All experiments are conducted on a single backbone (Step-Audio-2-mini/Base), single language (Mandarin Chinese), and a single in-house dataset; no cross-lingual, cross-model, or cross-domain validation is provided, limiting evidence for generality of the approach.

Reproducibility concerns: the MCLP pretraining relies on a claimed 300w (implied millions) hours of proprietary transcribed speech data, and the backbone Step-Audio-2-mini-Base is not confirmed to be openly available; combined with undisclosed hyperparameters for some components, this limits independent reproducibility despite the promise to open-source the dataset.

Subjective evaluation is based on a small set of 30 valid responses (out of an initial 31) rated by 32 annotators, and MOS explicitly excludes timbre/audio-quality judgments, so it is unclear whether the gains in perceived style come at a cost to overall audio quality/naturalness, which is not separately reported.

No comparison against alternative plausible style-reward baselines (e.g., speaker/style embedding similarity, CLAP-like audio-text alignment, or a trained style classifier reward) is included, so the specific advantage of MCLP over other feasible continuous reward signals is asserted rather than empirically demonstrated.

The content reward pipeline relies on a cascaded token2wav + ASR CER computation, introducing potential noise/error propagation from ASR that could bias the RL signal, and this source of reward noise is not analyzed.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not address relevant ethical/legal issues such as scraping and reusing copyrighted YouTube drama content and voices for training and potential redistribution as an open dataset.
Minor reporting/clarity issues, e.g., '300w hours' is ambiguous/likely a units error, and some notation (θ overloaded for both the MCLP model and the RP-TTS policy) could confuse readers.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and under-addressed problem: the lack of an interpretable, continuous reward/metric for stylistic consistency in multi-turn Role-Play TTS, as opposed to coarse emotion-classification rewards used in prior RL-for-TTS work.

The idea of using an LALM's own continuation log-probability of ground-truth audio conditioned on generated audio as a proxy for stylistic coherence is a reasonably creative repurposing of ICL capabilities, distinct from simple perplexity-based TTS quality metrics.

Substantial data engineering effort: a large-scale, richly annotated multi-turn RP-TTS corpus (scene + character profiles, speaker diarization, video-grounded scene descriptions) is constructed from real drama footage rather than purely synthetic dialogues.

The gated hybrid reward (MCLP + CER with a zeroing gate) is a sensible, and the reward-hacking ablation (style-only vs. content-only optimization) is a nice diagnostic that illustrates the trade-off clearly.
The pairwise win-rate analysis against human MOS (Figure 5) is a reasonable attempt to empirically validate correlation between MCLP and human perception, going beyond pure self-reported numbers.
weaknesses: The 'Information-Theoretic Analysis' (Eqs. 2–3) is unrigorous: the leap from conditional entropy to expected log-likelihood invokes an unproven 'small KL divergence' assumption with no empirical verification, and the claim that 'variation in MI is dominated by style attributes' because transcripts are identical is asserted rather than demonstrated (MCLP could just as easily capture speaker/timbre/recording-condition differences retained in TA4 tokens). This weakens the central theoretical justification for the metric.

The main comparison (Table 2) pits a model that is both SFT'ed and RL fine-tuned on the paper's own in-domain dataset against off-the-shelf, non-fine-tuned baselines (GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio, Step-Audio-2-mini). This is not a controlled comparison and largely demonstrates the benefit of in-domain fine-tuning rather than isolating the contribution of MCLP itself; no baseline is fine-tuned with the same SFT data but a different/no style reward for a fair ablation against competing approaches.

The paper motivates MCLP by contrasting with emotion-classification-based RL rewards (Wang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2025b), but never actually implements or compares against such an alternative reward empirically — the central claimed advantage over prior RL reward designs is argued only qualitatively.

Ablation in Table 3 shows the SFT-only model already achieves most of the MCLP gain (-4.829 to -4.725), while the subsequent RL stage with MCLP reward yields a comparatively small additional improvement (-4.725 to -4.636), and the 'w/o MCLP Reward' variant achieves lower CER and only modestly worse MCLP than the full method. This undercuts the claimed significance of the MCLP-based RL as the key contribution.

Subjective evaluation is based on only 31 curated samples (30 valid after filtering) from 32 annotators, which is a small and possibly non-representative set for drawing strong conclusions about stylistic fidelity across diverse multi-turn role-play scenarios.

MCLP requires a ground-truth reference recording of the same transcript to compute, making it a reference-dependent metric; this limitation (inapplicability to genuinely open-ended generation without parallel GT) is not discussed as a limitation.

Data provenance raises ethical/legal concerns: the dataset is built from copyrighted TV drama/YouTube content (character voices, likely identifiable actors) with an open-source release planned, but the paper's Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not address copyright, consent, or potential misuse for voice/identity impersonation in role-play synthesis.

Scene and character annotations are produced automatically via Qwen-VL and DeepSeek-R1 with no human verification of annotation quality/accuracy reported, raising concerns about label noise propagating into both training and evaluation.

Presentation issues reduce reproducibility confidence, e.g., ambiguous notation ('300w hours' for pretraining data), and reliance on a closed detail ('internal style classification model') for RL data filtering without further specification.
Generalization is unclear: all experiments are in Chinese (WenetSpeech-derived data), and no cross-lingual or out-of-domain results are provided to support broader claims of significance.

strengths: Proposes a novel, reference-based metric (MCLP) that cleverly repurposes the in-context/continuation likelihood of a pretrained LALM to quantify stylistic consistency, addressing a genuine gap (lack of objective style metrics for RP-TTS).

Validates MCLP against human judgment with a pairwise win-rate analysis (Figure 5), showing a sensible monotonic relationship between ΔMCLP and human preference, which lends empirical credibility to the metric beyond the theoretical motivation.

Constructs and will release a large-scale, richly annotated multi-turn RP-TTS dataset (1,435 hours, 311k scenes) derived from real drama content with scene and character annotations, which fills a gap relative to prior synthetic or small-scale role-play speech datasets.

The hybrid/gated reward design (MCLP + CER with thresholding) is well-motivated and the ablation convincingly demonstrates reward hacking under single-objective optimization (style-only produces gibberish; content-only produces flat prosody), which is a useful empirical finding for the RL-for-TTS community.

Strong quantitative improvements over multiple competitive baselines (GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio, Step-Audio-2-mini) on both objective (CER/WER) and subjective (MOS) metrics, including robustness in a cold-start (no audio history) setting.
weaknesses: The information-theoretic justification for MCLP (Eqs. 2-3) is informal: the claimed asymptotic equivalence between minimizing conditional entropy and maximizing expected log-likelihood, and the assumption that the KL divergence between model and data distribution is negligible, are asserted rather than rigorously argued or empirically verified.

MCLP as both evaluation metric and RL reward requires access to ground-truth reference audio for the target utterance, which limits its applicability to settings where references exist; this fundamental limitation (versus reference-free style scoring) is not explicitly discussed.

No comparison of MCLP against simpler alternative automatic style/style-similarity proxies (e.g., style/emotion embedding similarity, CLAP-style scores, speaker/style classifier confidence) to demonstrate that the added complexity of a separately pretrained LALM scorer is necessary or superior.

Subjective evaluation is based on a small set (31 curated samples, 30 valid after filtering) from a single language (Chinese) and single domain (drama dialogue), raising concerns about generalizability of both the dataset and the MCLP-human correlation findings to other languages, genres, or less scripted role-play scenarios.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section; the Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not address practical concerns such as copyright/licensing of YouTube drama content used to build and release the dataset, or the computational cost of pretraining a separate LALM (300w/~3M hours) for MCLP.

Reported MCLP values across models in Table 2 are numerically close (e.g., -4.849 to -4.636), and no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided for MCLP or CER/WER (only MOS has CIs), making it harder to assess the robustness of reported gains.

Reliance on a non-fully-open backbone (Step-Audio-2-mini-Base) and internal/undisclosed components (internal style classifier for RL data filtering, proprietary ASR for CER) may hinder exact reproducibility by other researchers.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: the lack of objective metrics for stylistic consistency in role-play TTS, motivating both an evaluation metric (MCLP) and a corresponding RL reward in a unified framework.

MCLP is a conceptually elegant and interpretable idea: leveraging in-context/continuation likelihood of a pretrained LALM as a proxy for stylistic continuity, with a clear formal definition (Eq. 1) and thoughtful design choices (e.g., choosing a semantic-token-based LALM to bias toward style rather than acoustic similarity).

Substantial engineering effort in constructing a large-scale, richly annotated multi-turn RP-TTS dataset (WenetSpeech-RP-TTS) with scene and character descriptions derived from real drama videos, including a well-documented multi-stage curation pipeline (Figure 3) and detailed statistics.

Reasonably rigorous empirical validation of MCLP against human judgments via a pairwise win-rate analysis (Figure 5), which shows a sensible monotonic trend supporting the metric's alignment with human perception of stylistic consistency.

Comprehensive experiments comparing against multiple strong baselines (GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio, Step-Audio-2-mini, and several Instruct-TTS systems) across both objective (CER, CAM++, Emo2Vec, MCLP) and subjective (MOS) metrics, plus informative ablations (SFT vs. RL vs. reward components) that convincingly illustrate reward hacking when using MCLP or CER alone.

Additional appendix analyses (cross-lingual generalization, breakdowns by scene category/turns/speaker count) add robustness and depth to the evaluation, showing consistent gains across diverse conditions.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/self-preference concern: MCLP is computed using a LALM initialized from the same backbone family (Step-Audio-2) as the RP-TTS policy model, and is then also used as the RL reward and as the primary evaluation metric for the resulting model. Although MOS provides independent validation, the paper does not directly address whether the MCLP gains are partly an artifact of reward-metric overlap or backbone-family similarity bias.

The main comparison baselines (GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio, Instruct-TTS systems) are not fine-tuned on the paper's own RP-TTS dataset, while the proposed method benefits from both in-domain SFT and RL on that exact dataset/distribution. This makes it hard to disentangle gains attributable to the MCLP reward specifically versus simply having in-domain training data that other baselines lack; a fairer comparison would include an SFT-matched baseline optimized with an alternative reward (e.g., an emotion-classifier reward as in prior work) rather than only ablating reward components on the authors' own model.

Details of the human correlation study underlying Figure 5 (number of stimuli, pairs, inter-annotator agreement) are sparse, and confidence intervals in the extreme bins are wide, raising questions about the robustness of the claimed strong correlation.

No sensitivity analysis is provided for key reward hyperparameters (C, λ, τ) or GRPO settings, leaving it unclear how robust the hybrid reward's balance between expressiveness and intelligibility is to these choices.

The claim that MCLP is "interpretable" is somewhat overstated; it is essentially an aggregate log-likelihood score without decomposition into specific stylistic dimensions (e.g., prosody, emotion, speaking manner), limiting diagnostic value beyond a single scalar signal.

The dataset and main evaluation are limited to Mandarin drama speech; the appendix's cross-lingual check is a small supplementary analysis (self vs. prev-prompt comparison) rather than a full validation of MCLP's use as a reward signal in other languages or domains (e.g., audiobooks, games) as acknowledged by the authors.

The code repository link is not provided in the submission (placeholder only), and several implementation details (e.g., exact prompt templates for all baselines, MCLP LALM training specifics beyond high-level description) would need to be fully released for reproducibility.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and under-addressed problem: the lack of an objective, interpretable metric for stylistic consistency in role-play TTS, and proposes a conceptually clean solution (MCLP) that exploits the in-context/continuation modeling ability of LALMs rather than relying on coarse emotion labels.

Provides a large-scale, richly annotated multi-turn RP-TTS dataset (WenetSpeech-RP-TTS) built through a non-trivial pipeline (source separation, diarization, scene segmentation, LLM-based scene/character annotation), which could be a useful community resource.

The GRPO reward design (MCLP + CER with a gating mechanism) is well-motivated and the ablation study (Table 3) convincingly demonstrates the reward-hacking failure modes of using either component alone, giving good insight into why the hybrid/gated formulation is necessary.

A dedicated human correlation study (Figure 5, 32 expert listeners with pairwise comparisons) is presented to validate MCLP against human MOS, showing an interpretable monotonic trend between ΔMCLP and human preference.

Comprehensive evaluation combining objective proxies (CER, CAM++, Emo2Vec, MCLP) and carefully controlled subjective MOS testing (with a gold-standard quality-control item and stratification by dialogue length), plus fine-grained breakdowns by scene category, turn count, and speaker count in the appendix.
weaknesses: Potential unfairness/confound in the main comparison: the proposed model is directly SFT+RL-trained on the newly constructed in-domain dataset, while most LALM and Instruct-TTS baselines are evaluated zero-shot/out-of-domain with only prompt reformatting. The large performance gap could largely reflect in-domain training exposure rather than the specific merit of MCLP as a reward, since no baseline is trained with the same SFT data but a different (or no) style reward for a fair ablation.

The RL reward ablation only removes MCLP or CER from the proposed hybrid reward; it does not compare MCLP against alternative reward signals mentioned as motivation in the intro (e.g., emotion-classification reward, or a naive similarity-based reward like CAM++/Emo2Vec used directly as RL reward). Without this comparison, the central claim that MCLP is a particularly effective reward relative to existing alternatives is not directly demonstrated.

The definition and justification of MCLP's 'reverse' continuation direction (predicting ground truth conditioned on candidate audio, rather than the reverse) is defended only by an appeal to intuition ('conceptually symmetric') rather than rigorous analysis or ablation of the alternative (forward) ordering; it is unclear whether the metric is truly symmetric in practice.

MCLP's dependence on a specific backbone (Step-Audio-2's semantic tokenizer, further trained on 3M hours of proprietary/undisclosed data) raises reproducibility concerns: the continuation-training data, its scale, and the resulting model are central to the metric but not released or fully specified, making independent replication of MCLP itself difficult even if RP-TTS code is open-sourced.

Language and domain scope is narrow (Mandarin drama only); the cross-lingual generalization check in Appendix B is a small, indirect proxy (self- vs. prev-prompt ranking on Genshin-Voice) rather than a validation that MCLP correlates with human judgments or improves RL training in another language, so claims of broader applicability remain largely speculative.

Key data-curation details are underspecified for reproducibility, e.g., the 'internal style classification model' used to filter 'Neutral' vs 'Not Neutral' samples for RL data is not described, and the extent of manual inspection/correction of LLM-generated scene and character annotations is not quantified.

No explicit code/dataset link is provided in the visible manuscript text (the sentence 'Our code is publicly available at' is truncated), which currently limits verifiability of the reproducibility claim.

The subjective evaluation, while methodologically careful, is based on a relatively small set of 30 test cases per system, which may limit the statistical robustness of fine-grained claims (e.g., MOS differences across dialogue-length subgroups) despite the large pool of annotators.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: the lack of objective, interpretable metrics for stylistic consistency in role-play TTS, which is distinct from existing emotion-classification-based reward proxies.

The proposed MCLP metric is conceptually elegant, leveraging in-context learning of a pretrained LALM to measure stylistic continuation likelihood, and is validated against human judgments with a clear, interpretable win-rate trend (Figure 5) showing strong correlation with MOS.

Thorough ablation studies convincingly demonstrate the necessity of the hybrid reward: MCLP-only reward leads to catastrophic CER degradation (reward hacking via repetitive acoustic patterns), while CER-only reward yields flat, low-MOS speech — clearly motivating the gated hybrid design.

Large-scale, carefully constructed dataset (WenetSpeech-RP-TTS) with a well-documented multi-stage annotation pipeline (scene segmentation, character profiling, speaker diarization), plus useful fine-grained breakdowns by scene category, dialogue length, and speaker count in the appendix.

Strong and consistent empirical results across objective (CER, CAM++, Emo2Vec, MCLP) and subjective (MOS with 50 trained annotators and quality-control gold-standard filtering) metrics, outperforming multiple strong LALM and Instruct-TTS baselines.
Supplementary cross-lingual experiment (Appendix B) provides some evidence that MCLP generalizes beyond Mandarin, strengthening the generality claim despite the main dataset being Mandarin-only.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation circularity: MCLP is used both as the RL reward and as a primary metric for demonstrating stylistic improvement (Table 2, Table 3), so the reported MCLP gains are partly a direct consequence of optimizing that exact signal; while CER and subjective MOS provide independent corroboration, the paper could more clearly discuss and quantify this circularity risk.

Reproducibility burden is very high: computing MCLP requires continuation-training a 7B LALM on 3 million hours of transcribed speech, and RL training uses 32 H800 GPUs for 1,000 GRPO iterations — this places practical replication out of reach for most academic groups, and no lighter-weight variant or ablation on the scale of continuation-training data is provided.

Baseline comparisons in Table 2 mix models with very different training regimes (zero-shot general-purpose LALMs, single-turn Instruct-TTS systems evaluated only in a favorable w/o-history setting, and the proposed model which is both SFT-tuned on the paper's own in-domain dataset and further RL-aligned) — it is not fully clear how much of the improvement stems from in-domain SFT versus the MCLP-based RL reward itself, since no SFT-only-on-same-data vs. RL ablation isolates this beyond Table 3's single ablation.

The theoretical justification for MCLP (that pretrained LALMs encode a continuous latent style space via ICL) is presented as a hypothesis and only indirectly validated; a more rigorous analysis of what stylistic attributes MCLP actually captures (versus purely a correlate) is missing beyond the win-rate correlation study with a relatively small pool of 32 expert listeners.

The dataset and full evaluation are restricted to Mandarin drama content; while Appendix B offers a promising but limited English/Mandarin comparison on a different (game voice) dataset, this does not fully address multilingual or domain-transfer generalization (e.g., audiobooks, virtual assistants) as acknowledged in the limitations section.

Details on inter-annotator agreement/reliability for the 48 valid MOS responses beyond the single gold-standard filtering item are sparse, and the number of test cases per condition (e.g., only 8-6-4-2 splits by turn count) is fairly small for robust subjective statistics.
